title: Working with creators in India: fit, briefs, contracts and ASCI disclosure
metaTitle: Influencer Partnerships and ASCI Disclosure Rules
metaDescription: How Indian brands find the right creators, write briefs and contracts, handle usage rights and payments, and meet ASCI's disclosure and AI-labeling rules.
lead: A creator partnership succeeds or fails long before the post goes live — in who you choose, what you brief and what you sign. In India it also has to meet ASCI's influencer guidelines and the government's endorsement rules. This is a practical walkthrough of all of it, written for brands rather than lawyers.
keyPoints: Choose creators by audience fit and comment quality, not follower count.
ASCI requires an upfront, prominent disclosure label on any post with a material connection — and free products count.
Video, Stories, live streams and audio each have their own disclosure timing rules.
Contracts should settle deliverables, approvals, usage rights, payment and takedowns before anyone shoots.
ASCI now expects labels on synthetic influencers and on AI-replicated faces or voices in ads.

sections.heading: Find fit before follower count
paragraphs: The right creator is the one whose audience already looks like your customers. Ask for screenshots of audience insights: cities, age ranges, gender split and language. A Jaipur skincare brand that ships across India cares about different numbers than a Lucknow restaurant that needs diners within a short drive.

Then read the comments. Real questions, inside jokes and repeat commenters signal a community; strings of emoji from unrelated accounts signal the opposite. Look at past brand collaborations too. Did the creator make the product part of a story or read a script — and did those posts carry clear disclosure? If you're weighing creators against paid ads in the first place, our comparison of [influencer and performance marketing for beauty brands](/industry-compare/influencer-vs-performance-beauty) sets out the trade-offs.
bullets: Sudden jumps in followers with no viral post to explain them.
High views with almost no saves, shares or meaningful comments.
Paid posts in their history with no disclosure — you would inherit that risk.
Health or money claims made casually in earlier content.

sections.heading: The core rule: disclose any material connection
paragraphs: ASCI's Guidelines for Influencer Advertising in Digital Media require every advertisement that an influencer, or their representative, publishes on the influencer's account to carry a label clearly identifying it as an advertisement. The trigger is a material connection between brand and creator, and ASCI defines it broadly: money, free products — including unsolicited ones — discounts, gifts, contest entries, trips or hotel stays, media barters, awards, and family or employment relationships.

Two consequences catch brands out. Sending free product and hoping for a mention still creates a material connection once the creator talks about it. And disclosure is required even when the review is honest and entirely the creator's own opinion. Only a creator who bought your product with their own money and simply likes it has no material connection to declare.

ASCI's permitted labels are Advertisement, Ad, Sponsored, Collaboration, Partnership, Employee, Free gift and Affiliate, along with Instagram's Paid Partnership tag and YouTube's Includes Paid Promotion tag. The label can be in English or in the language of the ad itself, as long as an average viewer understands it.

sections.heading: Where the label goes, and how long it stays
paragraphs: Disclosure must be upfront and prominent — hard for an average viewer to miss. ASCI says labels are likely to be missed if they appear only in a bio or profile, at the end of a post or video, behind a 'more' tap, or buried among hashtags and links. Platform disclosure tools should be used in addition to the creator's own label, not instead of it.
Responsibility is shared. ASCI holds both the advertiser and the influencer accountable: the creator makes the disclosure, and the brand must ask for an edit or deletion when a post falls short.
bullets: **Pictures or videos without text, such as Stories:** superimpose the label on the visual so it is clearly visible.
**Videos of 15 seconds or less:** keep the label on screen for at least 3 seconds.
**Videos over 15 seconds and under 2 minutes:** keep it on screen for a third of the video's length.
**Videos of 2 minutes or more:** keep it on screen for the whole section where the brand or its features are mentioned.
**Live streams:** announce the disclosure at the start and the end, and add it to the caption if the recording stays up.
**Audio such as podcasts:** announce it at the start, at the end, and before and after every break.

sections.heading: Health, finance, AI and the government's endorsement rules
paragraphs: Some categories carry extra requirements. Under an ASCI addendum dated 17 August 2023, creators who advise on or promote banking, financial services and insurance, or health and nutrition, must hold relevant qualifications and state them prominently at the start of the content. That means SEBI registration for stock or investment advice, credentials such as an IRDAI license or a CA qualification for other financial topics, and a medical or allied-health qualification for health advice.

Virtual influencers must also disclose that audiences are not dealing with a real human being. ASCI went further on 17 September 2026 with guidelines on labeling synthetically generated content in advertising, which take effect three months after publication. They make labels mandatory for synthetic influencers and ambassadors, for replicated faces or voices of real people even with consent, and for paid product suggestions made by AI tools, which must say 'Sponsored by' and name the brand. A label doesn't rescue a fabricated testimonial; that is prohibited outright.

Beyond self-regulation, the Department of Consumer Affairs issued its Endorsement Know-hows guide in January 2023 for celebrities, influencers and virtual influencers, framed under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It also asks endorsers to disclose material connections clearly and to satisfy themselves that the advertiser can back up its claims. Doctors face further limits from the National Medical Commission, which we cover in our [guide to personal branding for professionals](/insights/personal-branding-for-professionals). None of this is legal advice; for regulated categories, have counsel review the brief and contract.

sections.heading: Write a brief creators can actually follow
paragraphs: A good brief is firm on the non-negotiables and generous everywhere else. The audience follows the creator for their voice, and a brief that scripts every line wastes the reason you hired them.
bullets: **Objective:** what success looks like — trial, sign-ups, store visits or awareness in a new city.
**Audience and context:** who you want to reach and why this creator's audience fits.
**One key message:** the single thing viewers should remember.
**Approved claims:** what the creator may say about the product, each claim substantiated, and what they must not say.
**Disclosure instruction:** the exact label, where it goes and, for video, how long it stays on screen.
**Deliverables and dates:** formats, number of posts, draft deadlines, review rounds and the go-live window.
**Creative freedom:** what is open to the creator's interpretation.

sections.heading: Contract clauses that prevent disputes
paragraphs: Even small collaborations deserve a written agreement. It protects both sides and turns compliance from a favor into an obligation. Have a lawyer review your standard template once; after that, most campaigns only need a new schedule of deliverables.
bullets: **Deliverables:** formats, counts, length, platforms and posting dates.
**Approvals:** the number of review rounds and turnaround times on both sides.
**Disclosure and corrections:** the creator's duty to label, and to edit or remove content on request.
**Claims:** the creator sticks to approved claims; the brand supplies substantiation.
**Exclusivity:** whether, and for how long, the creator avoids competing brands — and the fee that pays for it.
**Usage rights:** organic reposting, paid amplification, duration, territories and edits.
**Payment:** amounts, milestones, invoicing and what happens if a post is late or canceled.
**Termination and takedown:** when either side can end the deal and what happens to live content.

sections.heading: Usage rights and paid amplification
paragraphs: Usage rights are where budgets quietly go wrong. A fee for a post on the creator's own account is not a license to run that video as your ad for a year. Spell out separately whether you can repost organically, run it as a partnership ad from the creator's handle, run it from your own account, and for how many months.

Ask for raw footage if you plan to cut several versions, and agree up front whether you may edit it. In light of ASCI's guidance on synthetic content, never alter a creator's face or voice with AI without explicit written consent, and label the result wherever the rules require it.

sections.heading: Payments, barter and paperwork
paragraphs: Pay in milestones: part on signing or draft approval, the rest after the post goes live and stays up for the agreed period. Ask for invoices, and keep the brief, approvals, final links and insight screenshots in one folder. If a regulator or a customer ever questions a post, you will want that trail.

Barter is still a material connection, so gifted collaborations need the same disclosure as paid ones. Creator payments and barter also have tax implications, including withholding and GST, so ask your chartered accountant to set up the process once and apply it to every campaign.

sections.heading: Measuring a creator campaign
paragraphs: Give each creator a unique discount code and a tagged link so you can attribute sales and sign-ups beyond the post's own analytics. Ask for insight screenshots — reach, watch time, shares, saves and link taps — within a week of posting.

Judge on cost per meaningful outcome, not cost per view. After a few campaigns you will know which creators bring buyers, and long-term partnerships with those few usually beat one-off posts with many. Our [influencer marketing](/influencer-marketing) team runs this end to end, and the [influencer marketing guide](/influencer-marketing/guide) covers selection and measurement in more depth.

faqs.q: Is #ad in a block of hashtags at the end of the caption enough?
faqs.a: No. ASCI says disclosure must be upfront and prominent, and warns that labels buried among hashtags or placed at the end of a post are likely to be missed. Put the label at the start of the caption and, for video, on screen.

faqs.q: We sent a creator free product without asking for a post. Do they still need to disclose?
faqs.a: Yes, if they mention it. ASCI counts free products, including unsolicited ones, as a material connection, so any post that talks about them needs a label.

faqs.q: Who is responsible if the creator forgets the label?
faqs.a: Both of you. ASCI places responsibility on the advertiser and the influencer, and expects the brand to ask for an edit or removal when a post doesn't comply. Write that obligation into the contract.

faqs.q: Do AI-generated influencers need special labels?
faqs.a: Yes. ASCI already requires virtual influencers to disclose that they are not real people, and its September 2026 guidelines on synthetic content make labels mandatory for synthetic influencers and ambassadors once they take effect.
